claims.text: Moderate thermal and mechanical loading promotes short-range ordering at grain boundaries in initially single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Grain-boundary short-range order eventually nucleates nanometer-sized intermetallic-like clusters.
The intermetallic-like clusters reduce grain-boundary cohesive strength.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion caused by ordering produces a transition from ductile to brittle fracture.
Conventional-alloy embrittlement is typically driven by segregated impurities or coarse intermetallic precipitates rather than grain-boundary SRO.
The proposed initial alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with minimal pre-existing SRO.
Aging at 600–700 °C combined with low-level mechanical pre-straining can stimulate grain-boundary SRO without causing full-scale phase separation.
The formation and connectivity of nanometer-scale grain-boundary SRO clusters mediate the proposed embrittlement.
Thermal and mechanical activation drives localized atomic rearrangement and chemical ordering at grain boundaries.
A critical SRO density exists above which grain-boundary regions lose ductility.
The loss of local ductility promotes crack initiation and cleavage-dominated fracture instead of ductile void coalescence.
Thermally aged and pre-strained samples will have lower fracture toughness than the untreated alloy.
Treatment will shift fracture morphology from predominantly dimple rupture to brittle intergranular cleavage.
Treated samples will contain a higher density of grain-boundary SRO clusters than the as-processed control.
The as-processed baseline exhibits ductile fracture and minimal grain-boundary SRO.
The proposed mechanism applies under moderate elevated temperatures and typical engineering strains and strain rates.
At very high temperature, under severe irradiation, or at very high strain rates, mechanisms other than SRO-driven embrittlement may dominate.
The critical SRO density or cluster size required for brittle transition has not been quantified.
The proposed effect may vary with alloy chemistry and may not generalize across high-entropy-alloy systems.
